title: Chapter 216 – The Keystone's Answer
html:
[The Wall – Han]

Han has commanded the Wall for eleven years, and in all that time he has never seen the Seam quiet for nine days.

He stands on the northern parapet at dawn with a cup of Qinghe's barley tea going cold in his hand and looks at the thing he has spent his life watching. It is not much to look at, from here. A long gray scar in the sky, a hand's breadth wide, running east to west above the northern horizon like a crack in old porcelain. Most days it hums. Most days it spits, now and then, a lick of pale fire that drifts down toward the Wall and has to be burned out by the tower's lamp. Most days there is the smell of ozone, and the taste of metal at the back of the throat, and the low continuous grumble of a thing that is thinking about eating you.

Today it does none of those things.

"I don't like it," says Qinghe.

She has come up behind him on soft feet, as she always does, with her hands wrapped in a dishcloth and a warm loaf under one arm. She is a short broad woman in a patched apron, with a face like a good loaf herself, round and brown and creased with laughter lines that have not been used in a long time. She cooks by sound now. It was one of the first things he noticed after the Elder died: the way she turned her head, listening, when she added salt, the way her eyes seemed to look a little to the left of whatever she was tending.

"Nobody likes it," he says.

"Wenyuan says it's holding its breath."

"Wenyuan says a good many things."

"He's usually right." She breaks the loaf and hands him half. It is hot enough to burn his fingers. "You've not slept."

"I've slept."

"You've dozed on the stair." She says it without reproach. "Eat."

He eats.

They stand together in the cold gray light, the commander and the cook, and look at the sky. Below them the Wall runs away to the east and west, a mile of black stone and iron, studded with beacon fires and the dark shapes of sentries, and on its northern face the old scars of ten thousand fires lie like writing. The tower rises at the center, tall and slim and faintly shining. It is the tallest thing on the Wall. At its top, behind a glass of pale fire, a man is sitting who has not stood up in a month.

"He asked for you," Qinghe says.

"Now?"

"This morning. Before the bell." Her mouth twitches. "He said, Tell Han to bring the sword. And to bring the boy with the bell."

Han lowers the loaf.

"What boy?"

"I don't know." She shrugs. "I'm only the cook."

---

The riders reach the Wall at noon.

They come down the north road in a long ragged line, forty of the Azure Cloud Sect in their pale blue, with a banner of white cloud furled on a pole. At their head rides a lean gray man on a bay horse, who reins in at the gate and swings down with the stiff dignity of a man who has been saddle-bound for nine days and refuses to show it. He hands the reins to a groom. He bows to the sentry at the barbican, a precise and courteous inch.

"I am Chao Wen of the Azure Cloud Sect," he says. "I bring a guest."

Han, who has come down to meet them, looks past him.

A little way behind the line, on a small gray mule, a girl of fifteen sits very straight in a stained blue robe. She has a bundle across her knees. Her face is pale and fierce and very tired, and her mouth is set in a line that tells Han all he needs to know about the last nine days. Beside the mule, on foot, a smaller figure walks. A child. A nine-year-old girl, in a cloak too long for her, with her hair in tangles and her arms folded tight across her chest.

She does not look up. She is staring at the ground.

"Elder Chao," Han says.

"Commander."

"This is irregular."

"Everything is irregular," says Chao Wen, mildly. "I have been informed, by a lady I should like to think of as honest, that the child is not safe at the Sect. I am told she may be safe here." The smile is thin. "I am not in the habit of discussing what I do not understand. I understand only that the girl in the saddle has not slept in nine days, and has said one thing to me, repeatedly, since the Hundred Stairs."

"What?"

"Take me to Wenyuan."

Han's skin prickles.

"She doesn't know him," he says.

"No." Chao Wen glances at the child. "But the child does. Or something in her does." He lowers his voice. "I would not, were I you, Commander, keep them waiting."

---

Han takes Lan Xiu's report in the gatehouse, over a pot of black tea, while the tower waits.

He does it because it is his duty, and because the girl will not climb a single stair until she has said it all. She sits on the edge of the bench with the oilcloth bundle in her lap and her hands wrapped around a tin cup, and she tells it in a low, hoarse, level voice, without once looking up: the Silent Terrace, the Quay, the five who are still stone. The old man who rubbed his eyes. The sound he made.

Chao Wen, standing by the window, does not interrupt. His face is gray. When she reaches the end he says, quietly, "Pei."

"Yes, Elder."

"Pei was the one who laughed at everything."

"She opened her hand," Lan Xiu says. "On the last night. I saw it."

The Elder turns his face to the glass.

For some time, there is no sound but the tick of the cooling kettle. Han, who has stood on a great many parapets with a great many grieving men, knows enough not to speak. Chao Wen rests one hand flat against the sill, as though steadying himself against a deck.

"I told Ye Shuhan not to go," he says at last. "I told him a month ago. I said, the Road is not for us. He said it was the only road we had." His mouth twists. "He was a good man. A foolish man. They are often the same."

"He left them," Lan Xiu says.

"He was ordered to."

"I know." She lifts her head, and her eyes are bright and very steady. "I don't hate him. I thought I would. I don't. But I want you to know it, Elder. When the others wake, I want somebody to have told them the truth."

Chao Wen looks at her for a long moment.

"Then I shall tell them," he says, "myself."

---

The tower is cold.

It is always cold. The Wall's stone is cold, and the Wall's air is cold, but the tower holds a deeper chill, a kind of stillness at the heart of things, as though the building itself were listening. Han climbs the spiral stair with a lantern in his left hand and his sword on his hip, and behind him, step by step, comes the girl with the bundle. The child walks beside her. Qinghe, who has followed without being asked, brings up the rear with her hands tucked in her apron.

He has climbed these stairs a thousand times. He has never climbed them with a child.

At the top there is a door, and he knocks.

"Come," says a voice.

Wenyuan is sitting where Han has found him every day for a month: in the high-backed chair at the center of the room, with his hands folded in his lap and his feet, in their wrappings, resting on a stool. The chamber is round and bare. A great window of pale fire looks out on the Seam. In the light of it, the Keystone's face is gaunt and calm and strangely young, a smooth young face under a cap of white hair, with eyes like two coins of moonlight. They turn toward the door as it opens. They turn, Han thinks, not to the man, but to the child.

"Ah," says Wenyuan. "There you are."

Mo Yan stops in the doorway.

She does not run. She does not cry. She stands very straight, with her small hands closed on the white bell at her chest, and looks at the man in the chair with the grave, level, careful look of a person judging the depth of a river. Then she says, in a very small voice:

"Are you the one who holds it?"

"I am the one who holds it."

"It won't leave me alone."

"I know." He smiles. It is not a Keystone's smile, Han thinks. It is the smile of an older brother. "Come here, child. Come and sit by me. You are carrying something heavy, and I would like to help you with it."

She crosses the floor.

---

Han has seen a great many things in eleven years. He has seen a Core cultivator burned to the bone by a lick of Seam-fire. He has seen the wall at Khorsa fall in a night. He has seen Wenyuan, white with fever, hold the line for nine days on nothing but tea and stubbornness.

He has never seen anything like this.

The child sits on the stool at the Keystone's feet, with the white bell in her lap, and Wenyuan puts out one thin hand and covers hers. They sit together in the cold light. For a long time, nothing happens. The only sound is the faint far hum of the Seam, and the shuffle of Qinghe, who has retreated to the window with her back to the room, and the pounding of Han's own blood in his ears.

Then Wenyuan closes his eyes.

The moonlight in them goes out.

It does not fade. It stops, like a lamp snuffed. For the first time in a month, the Keystone's face is only a face, the face of a tired young man in a plain white robe, and a long slow breath goes out of him, and the room seems to lean toward the chair.

"There," he says, softly. "I see you."

Mo Yan's breath catches.

"Don't be afraid. It is only me." Wenyuan's voice is gentle. "I am speaking to the girl in the bell. Sera, is it? Sera Thann. I knew your mother's name from the Founders' register. I should like to thank you for six hundred years."

The bell in the child's lap flickers.

A thin line of white light runs along the crack. It pulses, once, twice, and then a voice comes out of it, not through the air, not through the mind, but through the bones of the room: a child's voice, small and clear and very old.

Who are you?

"I am Wenyuan," says the Keystone. "I hold the tower. I hold the Wall. I hold the place where the thing you have been fighting reaches into our world." His thumb strokes the back of the child's hand. "I think you have been fighting it alone."

I wasn't alone.

"No?"

Mo Yan said she was here. The voice wavers. And then you said you were here, and it got quieter. It always gets quieter when someone says it.

Wenyuan is silent for a moment.

"Do you know what the thing is?" he asks.

It's a gift. The white line flares. It wants to give things back. It says it can give me my mother. It says it can give me a body. It says it only needs one thing, one small thing, and then it will let everyone go.

"What does it need?"

A name.

The word falls into the cold room like a stone dropped down a well.

---

Han does not realize he has drawn his sword until Qinghe says, quietly, "Put it away, boy."

He puts it away. His hand is shaking.

"A name," Wenyuan repeats. He has not opened his eyes. "A name that has been paid. A name that was given freely and then lost. A name, I think, that belongs to a child of nine who is not afraid." His voice is very even. "The Cartographer has been drawing it for six hundred years, hasn't he, Sera? Over and over. In a spiral. Because the thing in the Seam made him."

I don't know.

"I think you do."

The white line trembles.

It's Mo Yan's, whispers the bell. It's her name. But it isn't just hers. It's the one I had. It's the one my mother gave me. It's the one before I became a bell. A pause. It's every name that was ever paid. It collects them. It wants the last one.

The child on the stool has not moved. She is staring up at the Keystone's face, with her mouth a little open and her eyes huge, and Han sees that she is not afraid. She is something else. She is listening, with her whole small body, to a thing she already knows.

"What happens when it has the last one?" Wenyuan asks.

It stops being a Seam, the bell whispers. It becomes a door.

The tower is entirely still.

Han feels the words go through him like cold water. He thinks of the Wall, the mile of black stone, the sentries, the ten thousand fires. He thinks of Qinghe's hands in the dishcloth. He thinks of the child in the cloak, and the white thing in her lap, and the gray scar in the sky that has not hummed in nine days.

It was holding its breath, he thinks.

It was waiting.

---

The Seam wakes at the second bell of the afternoon.

Han is on the parapet when it happens. He has gone down from the tower to look at the sky, because he cannot bear to sit still, and he is standing with his hands on the cold stone when the whole length of the horizon flinches. He feels it before he sees it, a shudder in the air, a drop in pressure, like the moment before a hard blow. Along the Wall the sentries lift their heads. The beacon fires bend. The hum that has been missing for nine days comes back all at once, and it is not a hum, now, but a roar.

"To the walls!" he shouts. "All hands to the walls!"

The bells begin.

It is not an attack. He knows that in the first breath. An attack comes from the north, from the Seam's mouth, in great rolling waves of pale fire that break against the Wall's black face. This comes from nowhere. It comes from everywhere. It is a pressure in the stone, a tilt in the world, a single vast soundless pull, and the sentries nearest the tower are going down on their knees with their hands over their ears.

"It's the child!" someone screams. "It's the child it wants!"

He turns.

At the top of the tower, in the window of pale fire, there is a shape. Two shapes. A thin white figure sitting upright in a chair, and a smaller one on a stool at his feet. The light around them has gone from white to gold to a blinding, shuddering blue, and Han can feel, even from here, the heat of it on his face.

Wenyuan, he thinks.

Hold.

He does not know who he is speaking to.

---

In the high round room, the Keystone does not move.

He has not moved in a long time. He sits in his chair with the child's hand in his and the Seam's whole weight pressing on his skull, and he does the one thing he has been trained to do. He holds. He holds the way a pillar holds, without effort, without hope, simply because it is what pillars are for. The light beats on his closed lids. The roar is a wall of white. And at the center of it, thin and clear and nine years old, Mo Yan is saying, over and over:

"I'm here. I'm here. I'm here."

She is not saying it to the Seam.

She is saying it to the bell. To the thin voice in the bell, the one that has been alone so long. And the voice, hearing it, is doing something Wenyuan has not expected. It is not crying. It is not pleading. It is singing, in a high clear thread, one note, a note he has heard before, in the long dream of the tower, in the hour before the Elder died.

The Cradle.

He knows the words. He did not know he knew them. They rise in him from some place below knowing: eleven lines, in the Founders' tongue, as simple as a lullaby. We remember you. We have not gone. The door is open.

He opens his mouth.

And Wenyuan, the Keystone of the Wall, who has not spoken above a whisper since the day the stone took his feet, sings.

It costs him everything. He feels it go: the heat from his hands, the weight from his bones, the memory of his mother's face. He feels the moon in his eyes flare once, brilliantly, like a star going nova, and then gutter and go dark. It is not pain. It is simply loss, a long unwinding, like the end of a very long day.

But the Seam stops.

It does not retreat. It simply stops, the way a wave stops when it meets a wall, and hangs for a moment in the air, trembling. And in the silence that follows, thin and small and very close, a voice says, in the dark of his blinded head:

Thank you.

For what? he asks.

For not letting go. A pause. She's tired, now. May she sleep?

Yes, says Wenyuan. Let her sleep.

The light fades.

---

Han reaches the top of the tower a quarter hour later, with the stairs still shaking under his feet.

The room is full of smoke. The great window is cracked from corner to corner. On the floor, beside the high-backed chair, a child lies curled on her side with her arm over a small white bell. Her breathing is slow and even. She is asleep. Qinghe is kneeling over her with a blanket, and when Han enters she looks up, and her round brown face is wet.

"She's alive," she says.

"And Wenyuan?"

She does not answer. She looks at the chair.

The Keystone is sitting exactly as he was. His back is straight. His hands are folded in his lap. His white hair is a little disordered, and there is a small neat line of blood at the corner of his mouth, and his eyes, which have burned with moonlight for a month, are dark. They are two plain brown eyes, quiet and open and sightless, turned toward the window and the dying fire.

"Han," he says.

"I'm here."

"Is the Wall standing?"

"It's standing."

"Good." A long breath. "I can't see you. I thought you should know."

Han kneels. He does not know what to do with his hands. He puts them on the arm of the chair and finds that they are shaking, and that the thin white wrist beneath them is cold.

"It was worth it," says Wenyuan.

"Don't."

"It was." The ghost of a smile. "She will sleep for a day. And the Seam has gone quiet. I do not think it will be quiet for long. But it has learned something." He turns his blind face toward the window. "It cannot take what is held. That is the only rule I have ever really understood."

Behind him, in the smoke, Qinghe is humming.

It is a small, tuneless, domestic sound, the sound of a woman covering a sleeping child, and it is the first time Han has heard her do it in a month. He bows his head. He closes his eyes. And on the cracked glass of the window, in the ash of the last pale fire, a thin white line of light draws itself, once, slowly, like a signature, and goes out.

---

Night falls over the Wall like a lid.

Han sits on the stair outside the high room, with his back against the cold stone and his sword across his knees, and listens to the quiet. The Seam has not stirred since the afternoon. Down on the parapets the sentries have doubled. The kitchens have been turned into an infirmary for the men who dropped to their knees, and in the courtyard a priest from the Sect is leading, in a low voice, a prayer for the dead.

Nobody has died. He has pointed this out. The priest has said that it is good form, nonetheless.

The door opens behind him.

It is Lan Xiu. She has changed out of the stained blue robe into one of Qinghe's plain smocks, and her hair is wet from the washing-trough, and she carries the oilcloth bundle in both hands as though it were an infant.

"May I sit?" she says.

He moves over. She sits. For a time they say nothing, the old soldier and the young pupil, and he is conscious of the warmth of her at his elbow, the particular stillness of a person who has been awake too long.

"I want to give someone this," she says at last.

She opens the bundle.

Inside, between the last crust of bread and a lid of dark metal, there is a small flat book. She takes it out, and holds it for a moment, and he sees her thumb move across the cover as though reading it by touch.

"It was the Cartographer's. It has a song in it. Eleven lines." Her voice shakes. "He said it wakes sleepers. He said it had to be sung by someone who had paid. I paid. But I can't carry it. I'm going to forget the words, or I'm going to lose it, or I'm going to look at it and think of him."

"Then why give it to me?"

"Not to you." She almost smiles. "To the man in the tower. He sang it today. I heard it through the door. He knew the words without being told." She holds out the book. "I think it's his. I think it was always his. I think the Cartographer drew the map for him, and not for anyone else."

Han takes the book.

It is warm. The leather is soft as a glove. He does not open it. He turns it over in his big scarred hands, and thinks of the old man in the gray cloak, of the sound he made, of the stone mouth open on its final note.

"I'll see that he gets it," he says.

"Thank you."

"And the child?"

"She's asleep." Lan Xiu rubs her eyes. "She didn't say her mother's name tonight. She hasn't said it since the Stairs. I think she's afraid that if she says it, it will answer."

"Will it?"

"I don't know," says Lan Xiu. "But she told me something, before she fell asleep. She said she isn't going to be afraid anymore, because Master Wenyuan said she doesn't have to be."

"Wenyuan said that?"

"He said, I'm here." Lan Xiu gives a shaky laugh. "It's all anybody wants, isn't it? Somebody to say it."

Han has no answer. He sits with the book in his hands and the cold seeping up through the stone, and above them, behind the tower's cracked glass, a blind man and a sleeping child keep watch over the quiet end of the world.
